sections.heading: Synthesis methods
sections.text: 2.1.2 Synthesis methods The photochemical properties of quantum dots are strongly influenced by their shape and size, which are governed by synthesis methods. QDs synthesis techniques are generally categorized into two main approaches: top-down and bottom-up methods ( Yang et al., 2013 ). Top-down methods employ laser ablation, arc discharge, reactive ion etching, and chemical oxidation processes to thin bulk semiconductors to smaller diameters to form QDs ( Badıllı et al., 2020 ). Additional techniques include ion implantation, molecular beam epitaxy (MBE), electron beam lithography, and X-ray lithography ( Valizadeh et al., 2012 ). These methods enable the precise fabrication of QDs with controlled sizes and shapes, such as wires, tubes, or rings ( Mohamed et al., 2021 ). But their experimental instrumentation is more demanding. The surface chemical modifications are usually limited, and they are primarily applied to the synthesis of GQDs and CNQDs ( Chen et al., 2024 ). Bottom-up methods consist of small molecule precursors synthesized by wet-chemical approaches (microemulsion, sol-gel, hydrothermal or solvent pyrolysis, microwave or ultrasonic, and electrochemical methods) ( Korala et al., 2013 ;  Baragau et al., 2020 ;  Sobiech et al., 2021 ;  Chen et al., 2023 ) and aggregation by chemical vapor deposition (CVD). Among these methods, colloidal synthesis is widely favored due to the excellent dispersibility and low cost of the prepared samples. Under high-temperature conditions, precursors in solution decompose into monomers, which subsequently nucleate to form nanocrystals, the size of which is regulated by controlling the temperature, the reaction time, the concentration of monomers, and changing the surfactant ( Pasban and Raissi, 2021 ). Prepared QDs, particularly those with superior color purity, durability, and solution processability, exhibit high quality. Also, they have led to a rapid growth in the application of QDs in a wide range of fields, including bio-imaging, medicine, energy-harvesting devices, quantum information and displays ( Sung et al., 2024 ). However, bottom-up approaches often involve harsh reaction conditions and can generate significant by-products. Meanwhile, it's unsuitable for the preparation of QDs with highly precise chemical structures.

sections.text: 2.2.2 Synthesis methods The structure, crystallinity, and permeability of MOFs materials can change depending on the synthesis process and environmental elements, which can affect the functionality of the materials. Researchers have employed synthetic techniques such as hydrothermal/solvothermal synthesis, slow evaporation-diffusion synthesis, ultrasonic synthesis, microwave synthesis, electrochemical synthesis, and mechanochemical synthesis for the preparation of MOFs with excellent performance and structural designability ( Zheng et al., 2020 ). Among them, the microwave method is the most widely used ( Chen et al., 2018 ). Mechanochemical and acoustic chemical methods offer shorter synthesis times and greater environmental friendliness, but mechanochemical methods have a greater risk of generating amorphous residues ( Raptopoulou, 2021 ). Electrochemical technology has a short reaction time and a low required temperature, which is suitable for the production of large quantities of MOFs powders ( Martinez Joaristi et al., 2012 ). The hydrothermal method is less corrosive to the equipment, and the slow evaporation-diffusion method is not often used in the synthesis processes( Zheng et al., 2020 ). Based on the unique advantages of PC-MOFs over mainstream MOFs, a large number of scholars have carried out experimental studies and in-depth explorations with synthesis and application as the entry point, and PC-MOFs have increasingly become a hot spot for fluorescent materials research. Synthesis strategies for PC-MOFs with tunable structures and copolymers have been developed to ensure meticulous regulation of the degree of conversion of the MOFs precursors. In general, the synthesis process of PC-MOFs consists of two steps: The first step requires the selection of MOFs with suitable morphology and structure as candidate precursors ( Jiao et al., 2019 ), and the second step selects suitable conditions for post-processing the selected MOFs aiming at a partial rather than a complete transformation of the ligand and/or metal center. Currently, among the efficient PC-MOFs synthetic conversion strategies that can be employed, they can be broadly categorized into controlled pyrolysis ( Liu et al., 2019 ), wet chemical conversion ( Lu et al., 2016 ), and external field-assisted pathways ( Yi et al., 2020 ). Therefore, the necessity for a more profound comprehension of the properties of MOFs and their response mechanisms as fluorescent materials, in conjunction with the selection of suitable synthesis methods based on the physico-chemical properties of the analytes, will continue to provide feasibility and forward movement in the expansion of the fluorescence detection field.

sections.text: 2.3.2 Synthesis methods Chemical synthesis methods for MNCs require metal salts, reducing agents, suitable stabilizers and solvents ( Su et al., 2019 ). The main methods include chemical reduction, template method, microemulsion method and biosynthesis. Chemical reduction is one of the most commonly used techniques, in which NCs are synthesized in solution by reducing metal salt precursors. This method is easy to perform but presents challenges in achieving precise control over cluster size and distribution. The template method is a process in which the nucleation and growth of MNCs are controlled by the use of molecular or supramolecular templates. Although it is capable of obtaining clusters with uniform size and well-defined structure, its synthesis process is relatively complicated. The microemulsion method utilizes a microemulsion formed by a water-oil-surfactant system as a nanoreactor to limit the reduction of metal ions and the growth of clusters. This method can obtain smaller clusters, but the yield is low and not suitable for large-scale production. Whereas the conventional organic solvent synthesis method can produce a large number of fluorescent quantum, this method is toxic and thus unsuitable for biological applications. The biosynthesis method uses biomolecules or organisms to synthesize MNCs. It's green and the synthesized clusters are biocompatible, but it is difficult to control the size and clusters' structure precisely ( Zhang and Wang, 2014 ;  Chen et al., 2023 ). Therefore, the ability to develop non-toxic and green methods for MNCs synthesis has aroused great interest in the scientific community. Extensive experimental efforts have led researchers to incorporate natural and non-toxic substances into existing synthesis methods, enabling environmentally friendly synthesis by selecting safer solvents (e.g., water), green stabilizers (e.g., thiosulfate, phosphine, selenite, and alkynyl groups as ligands), and natural biomolecule templates (e.g., proteins, peptides, DNA, polymers, and plant-derived macromolecules) ( Ghotekar, 2019 ). In addition, the use of non-toxic reducing agents and energy-efficient techniques such as microwave, ultrasonic, and water-bath heating ( Naaz and Chowdhury, 2017 ) further supports environmentally sustainable synthesis. These approaches align with the principles of green chemistry—particularly 'Design for Energy Efficiency'—while maintaining cost-effectiveness. Therefore, by combining these green synthesis methods, researchers can explore high-quality, cost-effective and environmentally friendly MNCs and ultimately realize them in the field and large-scale production, which will help to go farther and farther on the road of green synthesis. However, current research has yet to achieve the optimal state of high stability, high quantum yield, and ability to precisely control the size and structure. Challenges remain in achieving precise and controllable modifications while balancing functionalization with the preservation of intrinsic properties, requiring continued and collaborative efforts from both domestic and international researchers ( Mittal and Gupta, 2023 ).

1 Introduction Pesticides are chemical agents designed to prevent, control and eliminate weeds, pests, and diseases, thereby safeguarding and promoting efficient crop growth ( Yan et al., 2018 ). However, with the rapid expansion of the scale of use, unlawful and excessive applications have intensified, making residue contamination increasingly inevitable. To ensure the safety of agricultural products, European Union Regulation (EC) No 396/2005 sets maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides in food. Exceeding MRLs can result in severely harmful effects on human health and the ecological environment. Many pesticides are resistant to degradation, leading to excessive generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) in plants, oxidative stress, DNA damage, and impaired photosynthesis, ultimately resulting in plant death and ecological imbalance ( Rosell et al., 2008 ;  Alengebawy et al., 2021 ). Furthermore, pesticides have been shown to persist in the environment for extended periods, with toxic substances penetrating and accumulating through the food chain. Consumption of pesticide-contaminated food may result in complex joint exposure patterns, potentially causing antagonistic or synergistic effects ( Lasch et al., 2021 ;  Lichtenstein et al., 2021 ;  Dobreniecki et al., 2022 ;  Yang et al., 2024 ) and impairing the human nervous and immune systems ( Casida and Durkin, 2013 ;  Xu et al., 2015 ;  Skolarczyk et al., 2017 ;  Huang et al., 2022 ). In the contemporary era, it is imperative to monitor and degrade pesticide residues to ensure food safety, environmental protection, and human health ( Yang et al., 2022 ). At present, traditional detection methods include Spectroscopy, Chromatography ( Xu et al., 2017 ;  Huang et al., 2019 ), Capillary Electrophoresis ( John et al., 2022 ), and novel analytical methods include Chemiluminescence assay ( Chang et al., 2023 ), Electrochemical assay ( Yu et al., 2022 ), and Colorimetric assay ( Gu et al., 2025 ). However, Chromatography is costly and cumbersome, while Capillary Electrophoresis requires highly skilled operators. Spectroscopy and Colorimetry lack sufficient sensitivity, whereas Chemiluminescence and Electrochemical assays, though sensitive, tend to be unstable ( Christodoulou et al., 2018 ;  Goh et al., 2021 ;  Wang et al., 2023 ). Consequently, it's vital to develop an effective method for the direct analysis of pesticide residues on-site. Fluorescence analysis, which utilizes fluorescence intensity to perform qualitative or quantitative analysis ( Wu et al., 2023 ;  Xiao et al., 2023 ), has attracted widespread attention due to its advantages, including rapid response, intuitive visualization, high sensitivity, ultra-low detection limit ( Li et al., 2020 ;  Zhang et al., 2020 ), and low cost ( Qi et al., 2019 ). With the development of nanotechnology, fluorescent nanomaterials have been widely utilized in fluorescence analysis ( Gemma et al., 2012 ). In terms of pesticide degradation, thermal processing techniques reduce pesticides but destroy nutrients in food. Biodegradation methods, while cost-effective, typically require long processing times ( Yashpal and Kumar, 2022 ). Chemical methods offer high efficiency but pose risks of secondary contamination. Physical methods are easy to implement but generally inefficient ( Bi et al., 2023 ). Therefore, the pursuit of pesticide degradation strategies that are both efficient and environmentally sustainable has drawn significant attention within the scientific community. Fluorescent nanomaterials have emerged as powerful tools for pesticide degradation due to their outstanding catalytic properties, reliability, cost-effectiveness, and rapid, high-efficiency performance ( Rani et al., 2024 ). In summary, the potential of emerging fluorescent nanomaterial-based technologies for pesticide residue detection and degradation is demonstrated. The efficiency and mechanisms of detection and degradation are largely determined by the specific types of fluorescent nanomaterials employed. Progress in developing novel materials with unique functions relies on a comprehensive understanding of fluorescent nanomaterials. This is essential to advancing pesticide residue research. This review provides a review of significant fluorescent nanomaterials, including quantum dots, metal-organic frameworks and metal nanoclusters, which have been applied for pesticide residue analysis over the past five years. It compares their structural features, sensing mechanisms, and synthesis methods, as well as performance differences, strengths, and limitations. In addition, the design strategies of new fluorescent nanomaterials aimed at improving detection and degradation efficiency in food were also analyzed. Finally, the review offers a summary and outlook on research progress, providing a theoretical basis for developing next-generation fluorescent nanomaterials.

2 Fluorescent nanomaterials Fluorescent nanomaterials are materials that are at the nanoscale or consist of basic units, typically ranging from 1 to 100 nm ( Nile et al., 2020 ). These materials exhibit unique characteristics as a result of their high surface area-to-volume ratio, tunable size, and adaptable physical and chemical properties. These features contribute to effects such as quantum confinement, surface activity, and dielectric-limited behavior ( Hamid et al., 2022 ). These materials have shown outstanding performance across multiple fields, including optics, electronics, magnetism, mechanics, thermodynamics, and chemical reactivity ( Gleiter, 2000 ;  Tran et al., 2012 ). A growing body of research is converging on the intersection of nanomaterials with biotechnology, artificial intelligence, electronics, materials, energy, medicine ( Park et al., 2021 ;  Kim et al., 2022 ), and consumer products, encompassing a diverse array of applications, including healthcare, environmental monitoring, industrial processes, and security applications ( Le et al., 2016 ). Fluorescent nanomaterials can be categorized by dimensionality or composition. Based on dimensionality, they are divided into zero-dimensional (e.g., quantum dots, nanoparticles, metal clusters) ( Almeida et al., 2023 ;  Chen et al., 2023 ), one-dimensional (e.g., nanotubes, nanorods, nano-bundles) ( Bergin et al., 2012 ;  Liu et al., 2012 ), two-dimensional (e.g., graphene, transition metal disulfides (TMDs), black phosphorus (BP)), and three-dimensional (e.g., nanocomposites, three-dimensional nanoporous materials) ( Pokropivny and Skorokhod, 2007 ;  Saleh, 2020 ). Based on material type, they include carbon-based nanomaterials (e.g., fullerenes, carbon nanotubes), organic nanomaterials (such as tree macromolecules, micelles, liposomes), inorganic nanomaterials (such as gold (Au) or silver (Ag), metal oxides, and semiconductors made of particles), and composite nanomaterials. Fluorescent nanomaterials are commonly detected through optical mechanisms, such as localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) ( Xiao et al., 2014 ), fluorescence enhancement, and surface-enhanced Raman scattering (SERS). They can also be sensed via changes in electrical conductivity, catalytic activity, ion-gating behavior, and other electrochemical modulations. In conclusion, due to the wide variety of fluorescent nanomaterials and their diverse sensing mechanisms, the selection of appropriate materials should be guided by the properties of the target analyte as well as the required sensitivity and selectivity for a given application. (2024) 2.1 Quantum dots (QDs) In recent years, QDs have emerged as highly promising fluorescent nanomaterials that have captured significant scientific interest. These nanoparticles exhibit quantum confinement effects and size-dependent photoluminescence. They typically consist of a semiconductor core and a shell layer ( Diroll et al., 2023 ) with multifunctional ligands encapsulating the surface. Their diameters generally range from 1 to 10 nm ( Vladimir et al., 2013 ;  Zhou et al., 2018 ), and they are often composed of elements from the III-V, II-VI, and IV-VI groups ( Mahato, 2017 ). 2.1.1 Properties and mechanisms In consideration of quantum mechanical principles, QDs exhibit distinctive luminescent and electronic properties ( Chan and Nie, 1998 ). (1) The chemical composition and particle size of QDs can be controlled to alter their fluorescence emission wavelength; a smaller QD increases the confinement effect, which raises the bandgap energy and causes more energy to be released in the form of low-wavelength visible (blue) light (Zou et al., 2024a,b). On the contrary, larger sized QDs have less bandgap energy and therefore emit red light; (2) QDs exhibit a broad absorption cross section, a high fluorescence quantum yield (40–90 %), and a molar absorptivity of up to 106 L/(mol-cm) ( Zrazhevskiy et al., 2010 ), this higher luminescence efficiency ensures brighter fluorescence signals, which improves the sensitivity and the signal-to-noise ratio in sensing applications ( Margaret et al., 2019 ); (3) QDs consist of non-reactive inorganic compounds and feature a protective outer shell, which grants them exceptional stability under light exposure. This structural advantage enables them to maintain strong fluorescence over extended periods, significantly enhancing the reliability of detection outcomes ( William et al., 2003 ;  Sun and Goldys, 2008 ); (4) QDs have a long fluorescence lifetimes of 20∼50 ns, enabling high temporal resolution for time-resolved optical imaging ( Walling et al., 2009 ); (5) QDs can generate light near electrodes in which an electron-transfer reaction occurs, and have been used as electrochemical sensors, optoelectronic devices and other applications in various fields. Based on these optical and electronic properties, QDs manifest distinctive sensing principles. The absorption of incident photons by QDs gives rise to electron-hole excitations and the subsequent formation of excitons. At the same time, these excitons exhibit enhanced stability as the carriers are confined within the quantum confinement of the QDs ( Wheeler and Zhang, 2013 ). Subsequently, the excitons undergo radiative recombination and emit photons of specific wavelengths, which are then conducted as signals via fluorescence quenching or fluorescence enhancement ( Nozik et al., 2010 ). The sensing mechanisms include aggregation-induced emission (AIE), photoelectron transfer (PET), fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET), and electrochemiluminescence (ECL). The selection of these principles is contingent upon the properties of the target analyte and the fluorescent materials to ascertain the mechanism of operation. However, because of the complexity of their structure, there are some challenges and barriers in the development of QDs applications. The high specific surface area leads to surface defects, capturing electrons and holes, leading to the change of spectral shape, the reduction of PLQY and photochemical stability, and so on ( Nazri et al., 2021 ). For this reason, scholars from all walks of life have improved the optical, chemical, and electronic properties of QDs through surface functionalization, heteroatom doping ( Nazri et al., 2021 ), establishment of core-shell structures, and complexation with other structures including graphene oxide and carbon nanotubes ( Hui et al., 2023 ). In addition to this, the size and shape, chemical composition, and structure of QDs, which affect their distribution, interaction, and degradation in organisms ( Dong et al., 2012 ), may cause oxidative stress in organisms ( Navarro et al., 2012 ). For example, graphene quantum dots (GQDs) can induce autophagy and inflammatory responses in organisms; Cd 2+  released from cadmium-containing QDs is released from aggregated QDs after surface oxidation, and binds to intracellular proteins or membrane structures, causing cytotoxicity and apoptosis ( Chen et al., 2012 ). For this reason, scholars from all walks of life have been practicing green chemistry by using CQDs, which have better biosafety, instead of metal quantum dots ( Sun et al., 2022 ). They used natural substances (e.g., plant extracts, food waste) instead of chemical precursors as green carbon sources. For example, Chandra et al.  Chandra et al. (2022)  successfully synthesized J-CQDs from the fruit of Jatropha curcas, which was used for chlorpyrifos sensing. However, there is still the defect of low fluorescence intensity in practical applications. To solve it, researchers carried out surface modification and functionalization, including doping, coupling, and hybridization with non-metallic or metallic nanocomposites.  Mei et al. (2024)  established a MnO 2  nanosheet (NSs)-assisted proportional fluorescence platform for dichlorvos detection using amplex red (AR) and CQDs obtained from okra. Meanwhile, it's unsuitable for the preparation of QDs with highly precise chemical structures. 2.2 Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are porous extended solids composed of metal ions or metal clusters coordinated with organic ligands, and are also referred to as porous coordination networks ( Furukawa et al., 2013 ). The first type of MOFs was successfully synthesized as early as the mid-1990s, and they have since emerged as a major focus of materials research. 2.2.1 Properties and mechanisms MOFs possess exceptionally high surface areas, uniform pore architectures, and tunable pore sizes, offering outstanding overall porosity. Additionally, their unique structure features atomically dispersed metal sites and customizable surface chemistry ( Gonzalo et al., 2022 ), enabling better control of interfacial separation and compatibility ( Cheng et al., 2017 ). As a result, MOFs have been widely employed in trace substance adsorption and separation, pollutant detection, catalysis, drug delivery ( Linnane et al., 2022 ), biosensors ( Chowdhury et al., 2022 ), optical antennas, energy storage and conversion ( Dolgopolova et al., 2018 ;  Xiao et al., 2020 ). Among them, MOFs can achieve more efficient and specific host-guest recognition compared with other fluorescent materials through stronger chemical tunability. Meanwhile, MOFs are characterised by an abundance of π and n electrons, a property that facilitates the efficient formation of variable fluorescence signals ( Wu et al., 2020 ;  Yang et al., 2020 ). Besides, the properties of MOFs make them mostly used as templates or precursors in practical applications. Researchers have employed structural engineering strategies, such as introducing hierarchical porosity or defects, and doping with heterogeneous metals and/or ligands, to composite MOFs with other materials and form functional derivatives with enhanced stability and improved electronic conductivity. However, some of the intrinsic properties of MOFs are unavoidably sacrificed due to the complete transformation of ligands and metal ions under harsh conditions. Therefore, to solve this problem, the researchers have constructed partially converted metal-organic frameworks (PC-MOFs) by integrating the structural advantages of pristine MOFs with functional derivatives of MOFs ( Zou et al., 2024a ,  Zou et al., 2024b ). Based on the unique properties of MOFs, analytes can form interactions with MOFs and transfer signals for responses. Currently, these interactions can be classified into four types, including direct changes in the MOFs material, direct charge transfer, photoelectron transfer (PET), and internal filtering effect (IFE). Meanwhile, the disparate interactions also cause differences in response modes, which include on-type, off-type, wavelength shift-type, and combination-type ( Wu et al., 2022 ). Among these modes, the "off" type is the most common. The "on" type is more intuitive and has recently attracted significant research interest. 2.1 Quantum dots (QDs) In recent years, QDs have emerged as highly promising fluorescent nanomaterials that have captured significant scientific interest. These nanoparticles exhibit quantum confinement effects and size-dependent photoluminescence. They typically consist of a semiconductor core and a shell layer ( Diroll et al., 2023 ) with multifunctional ligands encapsulating the surface. Their diameters generally range from 1 to 10 nm ( Vladimir et al., 2013 ;  Zhou et al., 2018 ), and they are often composed of elements from the III-V, II-VI, and IV-VI groups ( Mahato, 2017 ). 2.1.1 Properties and mechanisms In consideration of quantum mechanical principles, QDs exhibit distinctive luminescent and electronic properties ( Chan and Nie, 1998 ). (1) The chemical composition and particle size of QDs can be controlled to alter their fluorescence emission wavelength; a smaller QD increases the confinement effect, which raises the bandgap energy and causes more energy to be released in the form of low-wavelength visible (blue) light (Zou et al., 2024a,b). On the contrary, larger sized QDs have less bandgap energy and therefore emit red light; (2) QDs exhibit a broad absorption cross section, a high fluorescence quantum yield (40–90 %), and a molar absorptivity of up to 106 L/(mol-cm) ( Zrazhevskiy et al., 2010 ), this higher luminescence efficiency ensures brighter fluorescence signals, which improves the sensitivity and the signal-to-noise ratio in sensing applications ( Margaret et al., 2019 ); (3) QDs consist of non-reactive inorganic compounds and feature a protective outer shell, which grants them exceptional stability under light exposure. This structural advantage enables them to maintain strong fluorescence over extended periods, significantly enhancing the reliability of detection outcomes ( William et al., 2003 ;  Sun and Goldys, 2008 ); (4) QDs have a long fluorescence lifetimes of 20∼50 ns, enabling high temporal resolution for time-resolved optical imaging ( Walling et al., 2009 ); (5) QDs can generate light near electrodes in which an electron-transfer reaction occurs, and have been used as electrochemical sensors, optoelectronic devices and other applications in various fields. Based on these optical and electronic properties, QDs manifest distinctive sensing principles. The absorption of incident photons by QDs gives rise to electron-hole excitations and the subsequent formation of excitons. At the same time, these excitons exhibit enhanced stability as the carriers are confined within the quantum confinement of the QDs ( Wheeler and Zhang, 2013 ). Subsequently, the excitons undergo radiative recombination and emit photons of specific wavelengths, which are then conducted as signals via fluorescence quenching or fluorescence enhancement ( Nozik et al., 2010 ). The sensing mechanisms include aggregation-induced emission (AIE), photoelectron transfer (PET), fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET), and electrochemiluminescence (ECL). The selection of these principles is contingent upon the properties of the target analyte and the fluorescent materials to ascertain the mechanism of operation. However, because of the complexity of their structure, there are some challenges and barriers in the development of QDs applications. The high specific surface area leads to surface defects, capturing electrons and holes, leading to the change of spectral shape, the reduction of PLQY and photochemical stability, and so on ( Nazri et al., 2021 ). For this reason, scholars from all walks of life have improved the optical, chemical, and electronic properties of QDs through surface functionalization, heteroatom doping ( Nazri et al., 2021 ), establishment of core-shell structures, and complexation with other structures including graphene oxide and carbon nanotubes ( Hui et al., 2023 ). In addition to this, the size and shape, chemical composition, and structure of QDs, which affect their distribution, interaction, and degradation in organisms ( Dong et al., 2012 ), may cause oxidative stress in organisms ( Navarro et al., 2012 ). For example, graphene quantum dots (GQDs) can induce autophagy and inflammatory responses in organisms; Cd 2+  released from cadmium-containing QDs is released from aggregated QDs after surface oxidation, and binds to intracellular proteins or membrane structures, causing cytotoxicity and apoptosis ( Chen et al., 2012 ). For this reason, scholars from all walks of life have been practicing green chemistry by using CQDs, which have better biosafety, instead of metal quantum dots ( Sun et al., 2022 ). They used natural substances (e.g., plant extracts, food waste) instead of chemical precursors as green carbon sources. For example, Chandra et al.  Chandra et al. (2022)  successfully synthesized J-CQDs from the fruit of Jatropha curcas, which was used for chlorpyrifos sensing. However, there is still the defect of low fluorescence intensity in practical applications. To solve it, researchers carried out surface modification and functionalization, including doping, coupling, and hybridization with non-metallic or metallic nanocomposites.  Mei et al. (2024)  established a MnO 2  nanosheet (NSs)-assisted proportional fluorescence platform for dichlorvos detection using amplex red (AR) and CQDs obtained from okra. Among them, the oxidation reaction between AR and MnO 2  NSs increased the fluorescence intensity, indicating the feasibility of using biomass-derived cqd for pesticide sensing. 2.1.2 Synthesis methods The photochemical properties of quantum dots are strongly influenced by their shape and size, which are governed by synthesis methods. QDs synthesis techniques are generally categorized into two main approaches: top-down and bottom-up methods ( Yang et al., 2013 ). 3 Fluorescent nanomaterials for pesticide residue applications in food Fluorescent nanomaterials possess unique structural and physicochemical properties, offering significant potential across diverse applications such as biosensing, drug delivery, trace analyte detection, and photocatalysis. In this section, the potential of fluorescent nanomaterials for the detection and degradation of pesticide residues will be examined, highlighting their remarkable capabilities in this regard. It is evident that these applications have demonstrated encouraging outcomes and possess the capacity to transform the domain of pesticide residue research. A comprehensive literature review indicates that current research in this field primarily emphasizes detection and analysis, while further exploration is needed in source-level pesticide improvement and degradation strategies (see  Fig. 1 ). 3.1 Fluorescent nanomaterials for the detection of pesticide residues 3.1.1 Individual fluorescent nanomaterials Optical sensors utilizing fluorescent materials detect changes in fluorescence intensity resulting from sensor–analyte interactions, thereby producing quantifiable signals. As excellent luminescent materials, nanomaterials, fluorescent probes, aptamers, etc., can be used directly as optical signal sources or chemiluminescence enhancers in pesticide detection, and play a crucial role in signal transduction. Various sensing strategies have been employed, including fluorescence quenching/recovery, ratiometric sensing, stimulus-responsive fluorescence, and molecular recognition-mediated fluorescence response mechanisms. Among these, fluorescence quenching and recovery approaches are the most widely employed. For example,  Liu et al. (2024)  constructed a new approach for the rapid detection of clothianidin based on methylated lead halide chalcogenide quantum dots (MAPbBr 3  PQDs) through an electrostatic quenching strategy ( Fig. 2 a). MAPbBr 3  PQDs and clothianidin form complexes by hydrogen bonding or van der Waals forces, which increase the particle size and agglomerate with each other, leading to fluorescence quenching. This method is highly stable, fluorescent, sensitive, and applicable to other types of neonicotinoid pesticides using only a single quantum dot material, and can be extended to other types of neonicotinoid pesticides.  Sun et al. (2024)  developed an electrochemiluminescence (ECL) sensor based on tungsten disulfide quantum dots (WS 2  QDs) ( Fig. 2 b). The WS 2  QDs have a high quantum yield (QY) of 6.86 %, forming a co-reactive system with K 2 S 2 O 8 . The strength of ECL is enhanced through phosphate-mediated generation of more excited states of WS 2  QD∗ by OPs. This strategy not only achieves high ECL efficiencies, but also implements a green and sustainable strategy called ‘killing two birds with one stone’ ( Fig. 2 c). A silver nanoclusters (AgNCs) fluorescent probe that selectively responds to glyphosate was developed by Wu group ( Fig. 2 d) ( Mu et al., 2023 ). According to the interaction between AgNCs and glyphosate, the AgNCs were induced to aggregate and become larger to form large Ag particles, leading to fluorescence quenching of the system, thus enabling real-time monitoring of glyphosate. This study completes the evolution from two-step and multi-step detection to one-step detection, providing a creative way for real-time dynamic monitoring of pesticide residue distribution and metabolism in plants and vegetables. Fig. 3 For the past few years, the fluorescence quenching mechanism has been frequently used by researchers for the amplification of fluorescence signals due to its rapid, label-free and non-invasive nature, which avoids damage to crops and meets their detection requirements. Pesticide residues are detected accurately and sensitively by their degree of quenching. For example, Mahajan's team ( Mahajan and Patil, 2024 ) has developed a new fluorescent ‘switch’ sensor using an electrostatic quenching mechanism. The team synthesized water-soluble cobalt/zinc-nitrogen co-doped graphene quantum dots (Co/Zn-N-GQDs) for the identification of quinone pesticides in fruit and vegetables. Betel leaf was used as a natural precursor, with cobalt (Co), zinc (Zn) and urea (N) serving as dopant sources. Co/Zn-N-GQDs, which exhibit high fluorescence intensity in isolation, aggregate into Cu 2+ -Co/Zn-N-GQDs complexes in the presence of Cu 2+  through strong electrostatic interactions, resulting in fluorescence quenching. The complexes are disassembled by the addition of quinone, leading to the detachment of Cu 2+  ions from the surface of Co/Zn-N-GQDs, thereby inducing fluorescence recovery. In another study, Nair's team ( Nair et al., 2021 ) designed a fluorescent indicator based on sulphur-doped graphene quantum dots (S-GQD) and aptamer hybridization for the systematic detection of organophosphorus pesticide, leuco-methyl (OM) ( Fig. 3 b). The assay employs a fluorescence ‘turn-on’ strategy, in which unligand-complexed S-GQD aggregates with Apt, causing fluorescence quenching, and in the presence of OM triggers the decomposition of the S-GQD-Apt complex, transforming it into the Apt-OM complex and releasing free fluorescent S-GQD, leading to the restoration of the fluorescence of S-GQD. The method is doped with heteroatoms to reduce the bandgap and enhance light absorption to achieve the goal of ultra-high sensitivity and selectivity ( Fig. 3 c).  Su et al. (2022)  used a fluorescence quenching mechanism by combining an MOF and an aptamer, and designed an aptamer sensor based on GH-Cu BioMOFs and an aptamer as adsorbent and quencher. GH- Cu BioMOFs are adsorbed and the pesticide aptamer is adsorbed on their surface, leading to fluorescence quenching. Following the establishment of the pesticide target, the poor binding of the aptamer to the GH-Cu BioMOFs leads to a decrease in the adsorption of the aptamer onto the nanomaterials, and the fluorescence is switched on again. The most characteristic feature is the use of dipeptide glycine-l-histidine (GH) and divalent copper ions (Cu2þ) as bio-organic linkers and metal ions, which greatly improves its biocompatibility and reduces the impact on the environment. The method was successfully applied to the determination of the insecticide acetamiprid and has a high potential for application in the determination of pesticides in food and environmental samples. The use of a fluorescence quenching mechanism can achieve precise regulation and sensitive detection, and the research is moving towards a finer and deeper direction, which is expected to play a greater role in the development of new fluorescent nanomaterials and the innovation of biosensing technology. In terms of the types of pesticides and the harm they cause to human society, organophosphorus (OP) pesticides are currently the most commonly used, owing to their reduced toxicity and minimal residue. But sadly, as the most commonly used insecticides, OP not only exhibits neurotoxicity through inhibition of acetylcholinesterase, but also may lead to immunotoxicity and cardiotoxicity, and other adverse reactions ( Rajak et al., 2021 ). Therefore, researchers and scholars have conducted in-depth studies on the residue detection technology of organophosphorus pesticides, and have continued to innovate and refine the design and preparation of fluorescent materials with better performance ( Cai et al., 2021 ). However, most of the fluorescent sensors for organophosphorus pesticide detection rely on the inhibition of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) by OPs. For instance,  Yang et al. (2021)  synthesized cadmium telluride quantum dots (CdTe QDs) using a stimulus-responsive fluorescence strategy. These QDs exhibited a distinct fluorescence response under acidic pH conditions. Acetylcholine (ACh) is hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase AChE into CH 3 COOH, which lowers the pH and triggers a fluorescence burst in the CdTe QDs. In contrast, OPs inhibit this catalytic process, maintaining a stable pH and thereby preventing significant changes in fluorescence emission. This mechanism enables the detection of OPs. In addition, a novel dual-signal fluorescent sensor for the detection of OPs in vegetables was developed by  Wang et al. (2024) . The catalytic activities of AChE and choline oxidase (ChOx) were used to oxidise ferrocene-modified tetraphenylethylene (TPE-Fc) to TPE-Fc + , which aggregated to enhance cyan fluorescence. The simultaneous generation of •OH resulted in a decrease in the fluorescence of glutathione-synthesized gold nanoclusters (GSH-AuNCs), rendering OPs visible to the naked eye. But the inhibition of AChE is not only limited by the biological enzyme, which affects the stability of the assay, but may also produce false-negative results affecting accuracy. Therefore, to solve this problem,  Chen et al. (2024)  immobilised the enzyme in MOF materials and the enzyme triggered rapid nucleation of MOF, which could effectively improve the stability of the enzyme and the efficiency of cascade catalysis. They applied this approach to fruit and vegetable samples and constructed a cascade nanobioreactor for the detection of methyl parathion (MP) ( Chen et al., 2024 ). AChE/CHO and GSH-AuNCs were encapsulated in ZIF-8 as an immobilised carrier, respectively. This not only effectively protects the enzyme from the external environment, but also improves the catalytic efficiency and fluorescence intensity of the enzyme cascade reaction. This MOF-based enzyme stabilisation strategy ensures improved accuracy and detection performance of the fluorescent sensor, thus addressing the limitations of conventional enzyme-dependent detection systems. 3.2 Fluorescent nanomaterials for degrading pesticide residues Although real-time, sensitive detection of pesticide residues is crucial, directly degrading pesticides at the source is often more practical and effective. Instead of restricting pesticide use, it is more reasonable to develop robust degradation strategies that are both environmentally friendly and sustainable. Although degradation strategies are still underdeveloped compared to detection methods, increasing attention has been directed to this area. In recent years, the degradation of pesticide residues has emerged as a key research direction for fluorescent nanomaterials in agriculture. Pesticides can be broadly categorized into six categories: organophosphorus pesticides (OPPs), organosulfur pesticides (OSPs), organo-carbamate pesticides, organochlorine pesticides (OCPs), and pyrethroids, neonicotinoids. Depending on the target of the action, the target of the action, efficiency, and chemical composition vary. In general, common degradation methods include physical (e.g., adsorption, photolysis, pyrolysis), chemical (e.g., redox, hydrolysis, photocatalytic oxidation), and biological degradation (mediated by microbes, plants, or enzymes that convert pesticides into nutrients or break them down catalytically). Emerging technologies such as electrochemical degradation, ultrasonic degradation, nanomaterials degradation, and high-pressure processing (HPP) have attracted much attention in the scientific community ( Andreja and Sandra, 2023 ). Integrating multiple methods may enhance degradation efficiency while promoting sustainability, energy savings, and cost reduction. Currently, a large number of photocatalytic degradation strategies are used. Photocatalytic degradation is a process in which pesticide molecules are excited by ultraviolet light, undergo photoionization and homolytic cleavage, and are ultimately converted into environmentally friendly small molecules, which are classified into photogenerated electron-hole pair separation and direct oxidation of valence band holes ( Burrows et al., 2002 ). The photocatalytic decomposition of environmental pollutants is contingent on the efficiency of the catalytic materials employed; the development of efficient photocatalysts represents a highly effective method of environmental remediation. The development of efficient photocatalysts based on fluorescent nanomaterials has been the focus of researchers because of their excellent catalytic properties, mature and perfect preparation methods, good reliability, low cost, and high efficiency and rapidity.  Gaayathri et al. (2024)  ( Fig. 4 a) have extracted graphene quantum dots from rice husks at lower temperatures, whose electronic properties promote the direct transfer of certain carriers to the adsorbed pollutant molecules, and the generation of electrons from the valence band and into the conduction band under the catalytic action of light to form reactive oxidative substances or mineralized products, which were successfully applied to the degradation of three highly toxic organochlorine pesticides ( Fig. 4 b). Higher electron-hole pair separation provides higher photodegradation efficiency. At the same time, the use of rice husk as a raw material is conducive to large-scale production and waste recycling, and has energy-saving benefits while using energy efficiently. However, the degradation rate of graphene quantum dots on organochlorine pesticides is limited, only reaching 60 %–70 %, and there is still a large toxicity. The photocatalytic activity is closely related to the specific surface area, porosity, band gap and light absorption, and the composite fluorescent nanomaterials even showed excellent stability and recyclability after several photocatalytic decomposition cycles ( Heu et al., 2020 ), so  Targhan et al. (2024a)  proposed the use of carbon quantum dots containing a large number of sulfhydryl groups (CQDs-SH) as a passivating agent and designed a CQDs-SH/CdS quantum dot composite ( Fig. 4 c). The direct oxidation strategy of valence band holes was applied to enable the CQDs to generate hydroxyl radicals under light irradiation, which showed strong photocatalytic activity, thus completing the degradation of imidacloprid. The passivated CdS quantum dots could control their size and stability more precisely to improve the photocatalytic efficiency, which ultimately increased the photodegradation rate of imidacloprid to 88.06 %, solving the previous problem of low degradation rate ( Fig. 4 d). ZIF-CdS/Tpy generates electron-hole pairs under visible light irradiation and oxidises to produce a large number of hydroxyl radicals, which attack the C-N bond of imidacloprid adsorbed on its surface, thus completing the degradation. 3.1.1 Individual fluorescent nanomaterials Optical sensors utilizing fluorescent materials detect changes in fluorescence intensity resulting from sensor–analyte interactions, thereby producing quantifiable signals. As excellent luminescent materials, nanomaterials, fluorescent probes, aptamers, etc., can be used directly as optical signal sources or chemiluminescence enhancers in pesticide detection, and play a crucial role in signal transduction. Various sensing strategies have been employed, including fluorescence quenching/recovery, ratiometric sensing, stimulus-responsive fluorescence, and molecular recognition-mediated fluorescence response mechanisms. Among these, fluorescence quenching and recovery approaches are the most widely employed. For example,  Liu et al. (2024)  constructed a new approach for the rapid detection of clothianidin based on methylated lead halide chalcogenide quantum dots (MAPbBr 3  PQDs) through an electrostatic quenching strategy ( Fig. 2 a). MAPbBr 3  PQDs and clothianidin form complexes by hydrogen bonding or van der Waals forces, which increase the particle size and agglomerate with each other, leading to fluorescence quenching. This method is highly stable, fluorescent, sensitive, and applicable to other types of neonicotinoid pesticides using only a single quantum dot material, and can be extended to other types of neonicotinoid pesticides.  Sun et al. (2024)  developed an electrochemiluminescence (ECL) sensor based on tungsten disulfide quantum dots (WS 2  QDs) ( Fig. 2 b). The WS 2  QDs have a high quantum yield (QY) of 6.86 %, forming a co-reactive system with K 2 S 2 O 8 . The strength of ECL is enhanced through phosphate-mediated generation of more excited states of WS 2  QD∗ by OPs. This strategy not only achieves high ECL efficiencies, but also implements a green and sustainable strategy called ‘killing two birds with one stone’ ( Fig. 2 c). A silver nanoclusters (AgNCs) fluorescent probe that selectively responds to glyphosate was developed by Wu group ( Fig. 2 d) ( Mu et al., 2023 ). According to the interaction between AgNCs and glyphosate, the AgNCs were induced to aggregate and become larger to form large Ag particles, leading to fluorescence quenching of the system, thus enabling real-time monitoring of glyphosate. This study completes the evolution from two-step and multi-step detection to one-step detection, providing a creative way for real-time dynamic monitoring of pesticide residue distribution and metabolism in plants and vegetables. 3.2 Fluorescent nanomaterials for degrading pesticide residues Although real-time, sensitive detection of pesticide residues is crucial, directly degrading pesticides at the source is often more practical and effective. Instead of restricting pesticide use, it is more reasonable to develop robust degradation strategies that are both environmentally friendly and sustainable. Although degradation strategies are still underdeveloped compared to detection methods, increasing attention has been directed to this area. In recent years, the degradation of pesticide residues has emerged as a key research direction for fluorescent nanomaterials in agriculture. Pesticides can be broadly categorized into six categories: organophosphorus pesticides (OPPs), organosulfur pesticides (OSPs), organo-carbamate pesticides, organochlorine pesticides (OCPs), and pyrethroids, neonicotinoids. Depending on the target of the action, the target of the action, efficiency, and chemical composition vary. In general, common degradation methods include physical (e.g., adsorption, photolysis, pyrolysis), chemical (e.g., redox, hydrolysis, photocatalytic oxidation), and biological degradation (mediated by microbes, plants, or enzymes that convert pesticides into nutrients or break them down catalytically). Emerging technologies such as electrochemical degradation, ultrasonic degradation, nanomaterials degradation, and high-pressure processing (HPP) have attracted much attention in the scientific community ( Andreja and Sandra, 2023 ). Integrating multiple methods may enhance degradation efficiency while promoting sustainability, energy savings, and cost reduction. Currently, a large number of photocatalytic degradation strategies are used. Photocatalytic degradation is a process in which pesticide molecules are excited by ultraviolet light, undergo photoionization and homolytic cleavage, and are ultimately converted into environmentally friendly small molecules, which are classified into photogenerated electron-hole pair separation and direct oxidation of valence band holes ( Burrows et al., 2002 ). The photocatalytic decomposition of environmental pollutants is contingent on the efficiency of the catalytic materials employed; the development of efficient photocatalysts represents a highly effective method of environmental remediation. The development of efficient photocatalysts based on fluorescent nanomaterials has been the focus of researchers because of their excellent catalytic properties, mature and perfect preparation methods, good reliability, low cost, and high efficiency and rapidity.  Gaayathri et al. (2024)  ( Fig. 4 a) have extracted graphene quantum dots from rice husks at lower temperatures, whose electronic properties promote the direct transfer of certain carriers to the adsorbed pollutant molecules, and the generation of electrons from the valence band and into the conduction band under the catalytic action of light to form reactive oxidative substances or mineralized products, which were successfully applied to the degradation of three highly toxic organochlorine pesticides ( Fig. 4 b). Higher electron-hole pair separation provides higher photodegradation efficiency. At the same time, the use of rice husk as a raw material is conducive to large-scale production and waste recycling, and has energy-saving benefits while using energy efficiently. However, the degradation rate of graphene quantum dots on organochlorine pesticides is limited, only reaching 60 %–70 %, and there is still a large toxicity. The photocatalytic activity is closely related to the specific surface area, porosity, band gap and light absorption, and the composite fluorescent nanomaterials even showed excellent stability and recyclability after several photocatalytic decomposition cycles ( Heu et al., 2020 ), so  Targhan et al. (2024a)  proposed the use of carbon quantum dots containing a large number of sulfhydryl groups (CQDs-SH) as a passivating agent and designed a CQDs-SH/CdS quantum dot composite ( Fig. 4 c). The direct oxidation strategy of valence band holes was applied to enable the CQDs to generate hydroxyl radicals under light irradiation, which showed strong photocatalytic activity, thus completing the degradation of imidacloprid. The passivated CdS quantum dots could control their size and stability more precisely to improve the photocatalytic efficiency, which ultimately increased the photodegradation rate of imidacloprid to 88.06 %, solving the previous problem of low degradation rate ( Fig. 4 d). In addition to this, they also expanded a new idea to improve photocatalytic efficiency by improving its photocatalytic performance through ligands, designing ZIF-CdS/Tpy nanocomposite ( Fig. 4 e) ( Targhan et al., 2024b ). ZIF-67 with good adsorption properties, and tripyridine with remarkable photoluminescence and conductivity, they composite the two to synthesize a nanocomposite with better catalytic properties, superior stability and reusability, which was successfully applied to the adsorption and degradation of imidacloprid. ZIF-CdS/Tpy generates electron-hole pairs under visible light irradiation and oxidises to produce a large number of hydroxyl radicals, which attack the C-N bond of imidacloprid adsorbed on its surface, thus completing the degradation. While continuously improving the photocatalytic efficiency of nanomaterials, researchers also possessed new progress in the direction of exploring the multifunctionality of nanomaterials.  Ma et al. (2023)  used MOF-808 as a host and Fe-CDs as a guest molecule ( Fig. 4 f). 4 Challenges and future prospects Although fluorescent nanomaterials exhibit high sensitivity, rapid response, and ease of use in pesticide residue analysis, several significant challenges remain for their practical application. Firstly, fluorescent nanomaterials are environmentally unstable. Their optical properties degrade under harsh conditions—such as acidic or alkaline environments or heat—leading to reduced accuracy and reproducibility. In biological systems, their fluorescent behavior may be altered by enzymes, proteins, ionic strength, and other endogenous factors, resulting in performance loss. Structurally, their large surface area and abundance of active sites make them highly susceptible to environmental interactions, including agglomeration and chemical reactions with water, oxygen, or other substances, compromising their stability. Secondly, although organophosphorus pesticides have been widely targeted by existing nanomaterials, other classes of pesticide residues remain underexplored. The development of fluorescent nanomaterials for detecting or degrading these alternative pesticides is progressing slowly. Moreover, multifunctional materials capable of detecting or degrading multiple pesticide residues simultaneously are urgently needed to address the complexity of food contamination. In addition, the complexity of food matrices and background autofluorescence from food components further complicates detection. Most fluorescent nanomaterials require complex pre-treatment and the use of quenchers to reduce background interference, which significantly increases production costs and limits scalability. Consequently, many fluorescent nanomaterials contain heavy metals or toxic elements, posing potential risks of secondary contamination and environmental imbalance. These concerns contradict the principles of sustainable development. Therefore, the application of fluorescent nanomaterials must be preceded by thorough evaluations of their safety, environmental compatibility, and biocompatibility to ensure low or non-toxicity in real-world applications. Despite challenges such as poor anti-interference ability, limited functional capacity, high toxicity, and elevated cost, fluorescent nanomaterials still hold significant promise for future applications in pesticide detection and degradation. Advances in material innovation, multifunctional integration, and portable device development are expected to enhance their practical performance. These developments are anticipated to contribute meaningfully to both food safety and environmental protection. (1) Future development of fluorescent nanomaterials will require the careful selection of doping agents for functional modification. For example, rare earth elements can enhance fluorescence intensity and stability, while transition metals can improve selectivity toward specific pesticides. Moreover, composite selection is not limited to basic organic or inorganic substances or conventional nanomaterials. It also includes the exploration of natural, non-toxic materials such as microorganisms and biomolecules. (2) Ensuring that fluorescent nanomaterials are environmentally friendly and low in toxicity requires attention to both raw materials and synthesis methods. Green nanomaterials derived from plant or microbial sources are generally biocompatible, biodegradable, and effective in environmental remediation. These materials also support low-cost, large-scale production. Green synthesis methods, such as aqueous-phase or microwave-assisted synthesis, are encouraged to reduce energy consumption and align with green chemistry principles. (3) Develop fluorescent nanomaterials for the simultaneous detection or degradation of multiple pesticides and bifunctionality. Introduce a specific biomolecule, such as an aptamer or antibody, and use metal ions and enzymes as intermediate media to mediate the response of fluorescent nanomaterials to pesticides. In this way, instead of a single material responding directly to a single specific pesticide, a class of pesticides can be used as a target. Besides, photocatalytic nanomaterials, such as carbon dots, can be doped as guest components to achieve dual functionality through host–guest interactions. It is also essential to minimize autofluorescence interference by developing near-infrared or ratiometric fluorescent nanomaterials. Food matrices typically exhibit autofluorescence in the UV–visible range, and using NIR-emissive fluorescent nanomaterials can significantly reduce this interference. Alternatively, ratiometric sensing, which is based on the intensity ratio of dual-wavelength signals, can effectively mitigate autofluorescence effects. (4) The close integration of fluorescent nanomaterials with smartphones, or even with cutting-edge technologies such as artificial intelligence, robotics, the Internet of Things, and blockchain, holds the potential to transform data analysis, security, and sensor networks. Future research can focus on developing an integrated system featuring intelligent response, precise degradation, and self-regulating feedback. AI algorithms can be employed to predict degradation pathways. By constructing pesticide-responsive fluorescent nanomaterials and integrating them with Internet of Things technologies, real-time monitoring and intelligent response systems can be achieved. These systems enable dynamic regulation and on-demand release of active degradation agents, facilitating precise pesticide residue elimination. In addition, automated degradation devices, such as pesticide-degrading robots based on fluorescent nanomaterials, can be developed to enable fully automated residue management. In conclusion, it is anticipated that fluorescent nanomaterials will develop in increasingly multidimensional directions. To realize this potential, overcoming technical barriers and material constraints through continuous innovation and international collaboration will be essential. Such efforts will help expand the practical applications of fluorescent nanomaterials.

5 Conclusions This work reviews the recent progress in the application of fluorescent nanomaterials for the detection and degradation of pesticide residues over the past five years, highlighting representative materials such as QDs, MOFs, and MNCs. The photophysical and chemical properties, as well as the sensing mechanisms of different types of fluorescent nanomaterials, are analyzed to compare their respective advantages and limitations. Through an examination of design and synthesis strategies, it is shown that composite fluorescent nanomaterials can overcome the limitations of original components while retaining their intrinsic strengths, thereby broadening their scope of application. Furthermore, the future development of fluorescent nanomaterials is discussed, emphasizing strategies such as the creation of novel materials, multifunctional integration, and the incorporation of advanced technologies. These approaches are expected to facilitate the development and practical implementation of dual-function fluorescent nanomaterials for both detection and degradation of pesticide residues. The goal of this review is to provide a valuable reference for researchers in related fields, promote the advancement of pesticide residue mitigation technologies, and ultimately contribute to achieving a balance between environmental sustainability and human health.
